summary: Light first shown on Goat Island in 1823 at the mouth of Newport Harbor. The present tower is dated 1842, 1856, 1864 or 1865 by different sources. Keeper's house lost to a submarine in 1921.

lens.note: Original fourth-order Fresnel (archive). LighthouseFriends and Rowlett say a fifth-order Fresnel lens used here is at the Suffolk County Vanderbilt Museum; the present optic is listed as 250 mm.

structures.note: 29 feet from base to lamp (NRHP); 29 feet high (Lighthouse Board, 1894). Standing-tower date disputed: 1842 per LighthouseFriends, Rowlett and ALF; 1864-1865 per Visit Newport, NRHP and the 1894 report. NRHP description also gives 1856 for the replacement of the original lighthouse.
Two-story stone keeper's dwelling attached to the tower; struck by a submarine 1921 and torn down 1922 (NRHP) or 1923 (Rowlett)

access.note: Grounds open to the public; lighthouse closed to visitors (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett). Reached by a bridge from RI 238 onto Goat Island.

facts.agency: Coast Guard (owner); Friends of Newport Harbor Light (site manager, per Rowlett). Lease status disputed; see notes.

events.note: Tower built on Goat Island; Congress provided $2,500 in March 1823 (LighthouseFriends)
Activated New Year's Day 1824 (LighthouseFriends). The Lighthouse Board says the light was established in 1823.
Second tower built on a breakwater, by the Army Corps of Engineers under Lt. George W. Cullum (NRHP)
Light moved to the new 29-foot tower on the dike; $67,700 appropriated 1834-1842 (LighthouseFriends). Rowlett also gives 1842. Disputed with the NRHP's 1838.
Original 1823 tower dismantled and moved to Prudence Island (NRHP; LighthouseFriends)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaces the lamps and reflectors (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper's dwelling built on the granite pier next to the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends); Visit Newport gives the current structure as built in 1864
Present tower dated 1865 (NRHP); 'rebuilt in 1865' (Lighthouse Board, 1894). LighthouseFriends and Rowlett date it 1842.
Old keeper's house on Goat Island taken down (LighthouseFriends); NRHP says the 1838 light was taken down three years after the 1865 change
Changed from a fixed white light to an occulting light, fixed white for 15 seconds and dark for 5, from May 20, 1891
Keeper Schoeneman rescues sailors from a capsized launch of the destroyer Mayrant in the harbor
Keeper Schoeneman rescues a man from a powerboat drifted onto rocks near the torpedo station (LighthouseFriends only)
Keeper's dwelling foundation undermined when struck by a submarine on November 9, 1921 (NRHP); LighthouseFriends names the N-4 and says it rammed the breakwater
Light electrified after the dwelling's removal; operation turned over to military personnel at the torpedo station (NRHP). Bulletin 1922 lists oil to electric incandescent.
Keeper's dwelling torn down (NRHP says 1922; Rowlett says 1923)
September 1938 hurricane: serious damage at a number of Rhode Island stations including Newport Harbor (Lighthouse Service Bulletin)
Light automated (NRHP; LighthouseFriends)
Renovated by the Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends)
Coast Guard leases the light to the American Lighthouse Foundation; the Friends of Newport Harbor Light organized (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett)
Foundation announces a $120,000 restoration plan (Rowlett); LighthouseFriends dates the first phase to spring 2006
Foundation does not renew its lease (LighthouseFriends). Visit Newport describes the Friends as lessees; the sources disagree.

keepers.note: Roughly thirty-eight years at the station (LighthouseFriends). Rescues in 1912 and 1914 (Washington Times; LighthouseFriends). The 1894 report gives a single keeper paid $600 a year.

wrecks.outcome: Launch capsized in the harbor with eight sailors; Keeper Schoeneman picked up three, and boats from the submarine tender Castine, flagship Dixie and repair ship Panther took the rest to the torpedo station. LighthouseFriends dates it June 9; the Washington Times dateline is June 10.
Struck the breakwater and undermined the keeper's dwelling, which was then torn down. The nomination does not name the submarine; Rowlett says a submarine ran aground on the island.

corrections.why: The 1823 tower was moved to Prudence Island in 1851 (NRHP; LighthouseFriends), so the standing tower is not the 1823 structure. The NRHP and the 1894 Lighthouse Board report date the present tower to 1865. LighthouseFriends, Rowlett and ALF date it to 1842, and Visit Newport gives 1864. Editor to confirm the standing tower's date.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1823 matches the NRHP and the 1894 Lighthouse Board report ('established in 1823'). LighthouseFriends says the light was first activated New Year's Day 1824. Kept at 1823 with the 1824 date in the events list.

notes_for_editor: 1) Standing tower date: 1842 (LighthouseFriends, Rowlett, ALF, the Wikipedia lead which is not cited), 1864 (Visit Newport) or 1865 (NRHP; 'rebuilt in 1865' in the 1894 Lighthouse Board report). The NRHP is also internally inconsistent: its description section gives 1838 as the establishment date and says the original lighthouse was 'replaced by the present structure in 1856'; its significance section gives 1823 and 1865. The story leaves the date disputed. The proposed correction (1865) is for the editor to confirm. 2) Tower height: the record's 11.0 m is not confirmed; the NRHP and Lighthouse Board say 29 feet (8.8 m); Rowlett and the Wikipedia lead say 35 feet. Facts use 8.8 m. 3) Focal height: the record's 10.1 m (33 feet) matches the NRHP and ALF; the archive's 31 feet above water is a different figure. 4) Range: record 9.0 nm; ALF quotes the 2005 Coast Guard Light List at 11 nautical miles; NRHP and LighthouseFriends say eleven miles. Facts use 11. 5) Characteristic: the NRHP describes a green light; LighthouseFriends says green since 2005; the sources do not agree on when the colour changed. 6) Lens: the archive lists the original optic as a fourth-order Fresnel; LighthouseFriends and Rowlett describe a fifth-order Fresnel at the Vanderbilt Museum as 'used in' this light. The story does not resolve it. 7) Keeper's dwelling: the NRHP says torn down 1922; Rowlett says 1923. The 1921 submarine: NRHP says a submarine from the torpedo station; LighthouseFriends says N-4 rammed the breakwater; Rowlett says a submarine ran aground. 8) Lease: LighthouseFriends says ALF did not renew in 2018; Visit Newport says the Friends lease the structure; Rowlett (undated) names the Friends as site manager. The story says the sources disagree. 9) The hotel: the NRHP names the Goat Island Sheraton and LighthouseFriends dates the fill to the 1970s; the Wikipedia lead says 1960s (not cited). 10) Access: Rowlett says the lighthouse is 'accessible by walking through the hotel lobby'; Visit Newport suggests parking at the hotel and the seawall for views. Both point through private hotel property, so the story does not repeat them and gives no route. 11) The 1912 rescue: the Washington Times (June 10, 1912, p. 8) dateline says 'June 10' and names the Castine, the Dixie and the Panther; LighthouseFriends says June 9. OCR reads 'Castlne' and 'Rnd', so check the page image before relying on the vessel names. The newspaper calls the keeper 'Capt. Charles Schoeneman'; the archive gives Charles Schoeneman. 12) The 1914 rescue (Rose Island powerboat) rests on LighthouseFriends alone. 13) The 1838 Carpender report and the 1851 inspection quote come second-hand through LighthouseFriends; the original reports were not read. 14) The 1894 Lighthouse Board page is confirmed by the adjacent page header (249) as printed page 248. The 1892 report page (scan p. 19) has no confirmed printed page. The Bulletin 1938 page 40 text is interleaved OCR; check the image for the wording 'serious damage'. 15) Mary Ann Heath: a woman listed as principal keeper (1868-1873); the sources do not say how she came to the post. Lydia A. Crawford's relation to Henry W. Crawford is not stated in any source read. 16) The archive's contractors (David Melville, Horace Vaughn; no years) are not keepers and are not in the roster. 17) Newspaper searches run for this station: 'Mayrant' with 'capsized' (1912; the Washington Times hit was used), 'Schoeneman' with 'lighthouse' (1912-1922), 'submarine' with 'Goat Island' (1921-1922, RI; no hits), 'Newport Harbor light' with 'submarine' (1921; no hits). 18) No living persons are named: the roster ends in 1921. 19) No general period context is used. 20) Photos: none added. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the nomination's own dates (1838 active from; 1856 replacement; 1865 present tower) are now stated in the story. The Washington Times vessel names (Castine, Dixie, Panther) are read from OCR (Castlne, Rnd); the page image was not checked, so confirm 'Castine' before print. Visit Newport's 1960s landfill date is now stated against the 1970s from LighthouseFriends.
